title: Sanitation, Waste Management and Operational Intensity Across Motor Parks in Ilorin, Nigeria
content: Motor parks are high-activity urban environments where intensive passenger movement, transport operations, and waste generation intersect, yet quantitative evidence linking operational intensity with sanitation and waste-management conditions in Nigerian transport hubs remains limited. Understanding these interactions is necessary for developing targeted environmental health interventions. This study quantified structural and operational characteristics, waste-storage and disposal practices, policy perceptions, spatial differences in operational activity, and passenger utilisation intensity across six selected motor parks in Ilorin metropolis, Nigeria. A cross-sectional observational survey was conducted across six purposively selected motor parks representing public and private ownership structures. Facility-level data on establishment year, fleet size, daily passenger throughput, and passenger-per-vehicle ratio were collected. Among 72 surveyed participants, 36 respondents completed waste-management and policy assessment sections. Descriptive statistics, Wilson confidence intervals, chi-square goodness-of-fit tests, exact binomial testing, and facility-level comparative analyses were performed. Public parks had greater operational capacity than private parks, with mean fleet sizes of 45.0 ± 10.8 and 22.5 ± 3.5 vehicles, respectively, while private parks recorded higher passenger utilisation intensity (4.90 ± 0.14 versus 3.73 ± 0.43 passengers/vehicle/day). Fleet size strongly correlated with daily passenger throughput (Pearson r = 0.974; P = 0.001). Small waste bins were the predominant storage modality (22/36; 61.1%), followed by waste drums (12/36; 33.3%; χ² = 16.667; P < 0.001). Private waste collectors accounted for most disposal arrangements (33/36; 91.7%), and weekly evacuation was most common (28/36; 77.8%). Disposal costs of ≥₦5,000/month were reported by 27/36 respondents (75.0%; χ² = 15.44; P = 0.0015). Monthly sanitation policy ratings were favourable (31/36; 86.1%; P = 0.0014), whereas waste-commercialisation perceptions did not differ from a 50:50 distribution (P = 0.868). Ilorin South recorded the highest aggregate activity (85 vehicles; 330 passengers/day), and passenger utilisation intensity ranged from 3.33 to 5.00 passengers/vehicle/day. Motor parks exhibit substantial variation in operational pressure and sanitation requirements. Integrating transport activity indicators into sanitation planning, strengthening waste-service partnerships, and promoting resource-recovery approaches are recommended. Improved sanitation management in motor parks may reduce environmental exposure risks among passengers, transport workers, and surrounding communities while supporting healthier and more sustainable urban environments.
